blocks.text: Stomata (singular stoma) are tiny openings or pores in plant tissues that are necessary for gaseous exchange. They are typically found in leaves but can also occur in some stems. Each stoma is surrounded by specialised guard cells that open and close the pore; guard cells are bean-shaped, contain chloroplasts, and respond to environmental conditions. The opening and closing of stomata control the rate of transpiration.

During daylight the stomata open to let CO2 enter for photosynthesis, their opening being regulated by the guard cells. At night, when photosynthesis stops for lack of light, the stomata typically close to conserve water, although the plant still respires, taking in O2 and releasing CO2. Closing the stomata at night minimises water loss by transpiration.
The guard cells function as multisensory hydraulic valves. Two hypotheses explain their opening and closing: the starch-sugar hypothesis and the influx of potassium ions.

In 1856 the German botanist H. von Mohl proposed that the guard cells, alone among the cells of the leaf epidermis, carry out photosynthesis and produce sugars during the day. As the sugar concentration in the guard cells rises, their water potential drops; water moves in, the cells become turgid and the stoma opens. At night photosynthesis stops, sugars are converted to insoluble starch or used in respiration, free sugars decline, water moves out, the guard cells lose turgor, become flaccid and close the stoma. This mechanism does not, however, fully explain the rapid turgor changes of guard cells during stomatal movements.

The opening of stomata is brought about by the active transport of potassium ions (K+) into the guard cells, which lowers their osmotic potential. Water follows by osmosis, the guard cells become turgid and the stoma opens. Blue light enhances the process by acidifying the surroundings, promoting K+ uptake and water absorption. At night K+ diffuses passively out of the guard cells, water is lost, the cells become flaccid and the stoma closes.

blocks.title: Hormones and stomata
blocks.text: Hormones take part in stomatal movement. At high temperature, when leaf cells begin to wilt, the mesophyll cells release the hormone abscisic acid. It stops the active transport of K+ into the guard cells, overriding the effects of light and CO2 concentration, so K+ pumping stops and the stomata close.
Palisade tissue and the path of the gases

The palisade tissue lies just beneath the upper epidermis of the leaf. It consists of elongated, tightly packed cells rich in chloroplasts, arranged to maximise light absorption so the plant converts light energy into chemical energy efficiently. Carbon dioxide from the atmosphere diffuses into the leaf through the stomata, travels through the air spaces of the spongy mesophyll into the palisade cells, and is used in photosynthesis. The oxygen produced diffuses out of the palisade cells back through the spongy mesophyll and leaves through the stomata.

blocks.alt: A leaf in cross-section: a waxy cuticle over the upper epidermis, a row of tall palisade cells full of chloroplasts, loosely packed round spongy cells with air spaces, and a lower epidermis with a pair of bean-shaped guard cells around a stoma; arrows show carbon dioxide entering and oxygen and water leaving. Inset: a stoma open between turgid guard cells and closed between flaccid ones.
blocks.caption: Structure of a leaf and the opening and closing of a stoma (original diagram after Figures 8.4 and 8.5).
blocks.long_description: The cuticle and upper epidermis cover a palisade layer of tightly packed, chloroplast-rich cells where most photosynthesis happens, above a spongy layer with air spaces. In the lower epidermis two bean-shaped guard cells with chloroplasts surround each stoma. Carbon dioxide diffuses in through the stoma and the air spaces to the palisade cells, and oxygen and water vapour leave the same way. When K+ and water enter the guard cells they become turgid and the stoma opens; when they leave the cells go flaccid and the stoma closes.

blocks.prompt: Explain why a wilting leaf on a hot afternoon closes its stomata even though the light and CO2 conditions favour opening.
blocks.explanation: The mesophyll cells of the wilting leaf release abscisic acid, which stops the active transport of K+ into the guard cells. Without the K+ influx no water enters, the guard cells lose turgor and become flaccid, and the stomata close, overriding the effects of light and CO2.

items: Stomata are pores, mostly in leaves, between two bean-shaped, chloroplast-bearing guard cells; they open by day for CO2 and close at night to save water, controlling transpiration.

Starch-sugar hypothesis: guard cell sugars rise by day, lowering water potential so water enters and the cells turn turgid. K+ influx: active transport of K+ (enhanced by blue light) draws water in; at night K+ leaks out. Abscisic acid stops K+ pumping in wilting leaves.
Palisade cells under the upper epidermis are packed with chloroplasts; CO2 reaches them through the stomata and spongy air spaces, and O2 leaves the same way.
